content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›CouchDB Selectors

Using stub.GetQueryResult()

The stub.GetQueryResult() function is your gateway to rich queries. It accepts a CouchDB selector string, which is a JSON object defining your query criteria.

Best Practice

Always include a docType field in your asset structs. This allows you to filter for specific asset types, preventing unintended query results.

Key Takeaway

CouchDB selectors, combined with docType, enable precise and efficient filtering of ledger data.

Example: CouchDB Selector

{
  "selector": {
    "docType": "car",
    "color": "red",
    "owner": "Alice",
    "value": { "$gt": 15000 }
  }
}

This selector finds all documents where:

  • •docType is "car"
  • •color is "red"
  • •owner is "Alice"
  • •value is greater than 15000

screens.title: Optimizing Rich Queries with Indexes
screens.narratorSegment: While rich queries offer immense flexibility, their performance can suffer significantly without proper optimization. This is where CouchDB indexes become absolutely critical. An index is a special lookup table that the database can use to speed up data retrieval. Without indexes, CouchDB would have to scan every single document in the ledger to find matches for your query, which is incredibly slow and resource-intensive, especially on large ledgers. Think of it like trying to find a specific page in a book without an index or table of contents; you'd have to read every page. Indexes are typically defined in JSON files and deployed alongside your chaincode. They specify which fields your queries will frequently target, allowing CouchDB to build an efficient data structure for those lookups. Remember, rich queries are only supported with CouchDB; if your network uses LevelDB, you're limited to key-based queries and range queries. Always plan your indexes based on your expected query patterns to ensure optimal performance. Optimizing Rich Queries with Indexes means couchdb indexes are essential for efficient rich queries, preventing full ledger scans and performance bottlenecks.. In practical terms, the critical role of couchdb indexes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›CouchDB Indexes

Why Indexes are Crucial

  • •Without indexes, rich queries can be very slow and resource-intensive.
  • •CouchDB would perform full ledger scans, impacting performance on large datasets.
  • •Indexes are deployed as JSON files alongside your chaincode.
Important Note

Rich queries and indexes are only supported when your Hyperledger Fabric network uses CouchDB as its state database. LevelDB is limited to key-based queries.

Key Takeaway

Always define appropriate CouchDB indexes for frequently queried fields to ensure optimal chaincode performance and scalability.

Example: CouchDB Index Definition

// META-INF/statedb/couchdb/indexes/indexCarOwner.json
{
  "index": {
    "fields": ["docType", "owner"]
  },
  "ddoc": "indexCarOwnerDoc",
  "name": "indexCarOwner",
  "type": "json"
}

This index allows efficient queries on:

  • •docType field
  • •owner field

It's crucial to match your index fields to your common query patterns.

screens.title: Private Data Collections: Confidentiality by Design
screens.narratorSegment: Confidentiality is a paramount concern in many enterprise blockchain use cases. While the main ledger, or world state, is visible to all organizations on a channel, there are often situations where sensitive information needs to be shared only among a subset of those organizations. This is precisely the problem that Private Data Collections, or PDCs, solve in Hyperledger Fabric. PDCs allow specific data to remain confidential from the broader network, visible only to authorized peers. For example, imagine a supply chain where pricing agreements between a manufacturer and a distributor should not be visible to other participants. With PDCs, the actual sensitive data is stored on the private databases of the authorized peers, and only a cryptographic hash of this private data is committed to the main channel ledger. This hash serves as an immutable, verifiable record without revealing the underlying sensitive details, ensuring both privacy and integrity. This mechanism is critical for maintaining business confidentiality in a transparent blockchain environment. Private Data Collections: Confidentiality by Design means pdcs enable confidential data sharing among a subset of organizations, with only a hash on the public ledger.. In practical terms, sharing data confidentially among select organizations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›Private Data Collections

The Need for Confidentiality

  • •Main ledger data is visible to all organizations on a channel.
  • •Sensitive information (e.g., pricing, health records) needs restricted visibility.
  • •PDCs allow a subset of organizations to keep data confidential.
How PDCs Work

Data in a PDC is stored on authorized peers' private databases. Only a hash of this private data is committed to the main channel ledger as an immutable record, ensuring privacy and integrity.

Key Takeaway

PDCs are essential for maintaining business confidentiality in Hyperledger Fabric, enabling selective data sharing while preserving ledger integrity.

keyIdea.text: Use `stub.PutPrivateData()`, `stub.GetPrivateData()`, and `stub.DelPrivateData()` with a `collection` argument for confidential data.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›PDC Operations

Dedicated Functions for PDCs

  • •stub.PutPrivateData(collection, key, value): Stores data.
  • •stub.GetPrivateData(collection, key): Retrieves data.
  • •stub.DelPrivateData(collection, key): Deletes data.
Critical Warning

Never store private data directly on the public ledger. Always use the dedicated PutPrivateData function and ensure your collection configuration is correct to prevent data leakage.

Key Takeaway

Always use the specific stub.PutPrivateData(), GetPrivateData(), and DelPrivateData() functions with the correct collection argument for confidential data.

Code Example: Storing Private Data

// Store private data in 'myPrivateCollection'
collectionName := "myPrivateCollection"
assetID := "asset123"
privateData := []byte("{\"creditScore\": 750}")

err := stub.PutPrivateData(collectionName, assetID, privateData)
if err != nil {
    // Handle error
    return shim.Error("Failed to put private data")
}

This snippet demonstrates how to store a JSON object representing a credit score into a private collection. The collectionName argument is crucial for directing the data to the correct private database.

screens.title: Configuring Private Data Collections
screens.narratorSegment: Before your chaincode can interact with Private Data Collections, you need to define them. This is done through a collection configuration file, typically in YAML format, which specifies the rules for each collection. This configuration is deployed alongside your chaincode and dictates which organizations are authorized to store and access data within that collection. Key elements in the configuration include the name of the collection, a policy that defines the endorsement rules for private data transactions, and other parameters like required Peer Count, max Peer Count, and block To Live. The policy is particularly important as it uses MSP IDs to explicitly list which organizations are members of the collection and can therefore see the private data. For example, a policy like 'OR('Org1MSP. member', 'Org2MSP. member')' means that members from either Org1 or Org2 can transact within this collection. This granular control ensures that data confidentiality is enforced at the network level, not just within the chaincode logic. Proper configuration is vital for the security and functionality of your PDCs. Configuring Private Data Collections means pdc configuration files define collection rules, including authorized organizations and data lifecycle, deployed with chaincode.. In practical terms, specifying authorized organizations and data lifecycle. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3›Chapter 3.3›PDC Configuration

Defining Collection Rules

  • •Collection configuration files (e.g., YAML) define PDC rules.
  • •Specifies authorized organizations and data lifecycle parameters.
  • •Deployed alongside your chaincode.
Policy Importance

The policy field uses MSP IDs to explicitly define which organizations are members of the collection and can access the private data, ensuring network-level confidentiality.

Key Takeaway

Properly configuring your Private Data Collections with clear policies is crucial for enforcing data confidentiality and access control at the network level.

Example: Collection Configuration

# collections.json
[
  {
    "name": "assetPrivateDetailsCollection",
    "policy": "OR('Org1MSP.member', 'Org2MSP.member')",
    "requiredPeerCount": 0,
    "maxPeerCount": 3,
    "blockToLive": 0,
    "memberOnlyRead": true
  }
]

This configuration defines a collection where members of Org1MSP or Org2MSP can transact. The policy field is key to defining access.

screens.title: Fine-Grained Access Control with Client Identity
screens.narratorSegment: Access control is a cornerstone of any secure enterprise application, and blockchain is no exception. Module 3›Chapter 3.3›CID Functions

Key CID Functions

  • •stub.GetCreator(): Raw identity of transaction creator.
  • •cid.GetID(): Unique ID of the client.
  • •cid.GetMSPID(): MSP ID of the client's organization.
  • •cid.AssertAttributeValue(name, value): Checks for specific attribute.
  • •cid.GetAttributeValue(name): Retrieves attribute value.
Use Case

Restrict functions to specific organizations or users based on their MSP ID or X.509 certificate attributes.

Key Takeaway

CID functions provide the tools to implement robust, identity-based access control directly within your chaincode logic.

Code Example: Restricting by MSP ID

func (s *SimpleChaincode) restrictedFunction(stub shim.ChaincodeStubInterface, args []string) peer.Response {
    id, err := cid.New(stub)
    if err != nil {
        return shim.Error("Failed to get client identity: " + err.Error())
    }

    mspID, err := id.GetMSPID()
    if err != nil {
        return shim.Error("Failed to get MSP ID: " + err.Error())
    }

    if mspID != "Org1MSP" {
        return shim.Error("Unauthorized: Only Org1MSP members can execute this function.")
    }
    // ... continue with function logic
    return shim.Success(nil)
}

This Go example demonstrates how to check the transaction creator's MSP ID and return an error if they are not from "Org1MSP", effectively restricting access.

screens.title: Ensuring Chaincode Security and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond the initial pitfalls, several other critical considerations ensure the long-term security and performance of your chaincode. Replay attacks, where identical transactions are re-submitted to have different effects, must be prevented. Fabric's transaction ID helps, but your chaincode logic should also account for this. Beyond the initial pitfalls, several other critical considerations ensure the long-term security and performance of your chaincode. Replay attacks, where identical transactions are re-submitted to have different effects, must be prevented. Fabric's transaction ID helps, but your chaincode logic should also account for this. Next, be wary of infinite loops or resource exhaustion. Complex loops or recursive calls can lead to timeouts or consume excessive peer resources, destabilizing your network. Design your logic to be efficient and bounded, especially when processing large datasets. Finally, avoid external dependencies. Making external network calls, such as HTTP requests, from chaincode introduces non-determinism, which is a major no-go for blockchain. If external data is needed, it should be provided deterministically as part of the transaction proposal or through a trusted oracle pattern. By diligently addressing these advanced security and performance considerations, you can build truly robust, reliable, and production-ready Hyperledger Fabric applications.
